_meta.note: Care values are deliberately conservative ranges, not single numbers. Houseplant care varies with pot size, substrate, airflow and season; a card that states '7 days' is wrong for most readers. Toxicity flags follow ASPGA/ASPCA-style classification for cats and dogs and should be re-verified before any claim is printed.

species.light: Bright indirect. Tolerates a few hours of soft morning sun; harsh afternoon sun scorches leaves.
species.water: Water when the top 2 inches of soil are dry. Drench until it runs from the drainage hole, then let it drain fully.
species.soil: Chunky, fast-draining mix — potting soil with bark and perlite.
species.feeding: Balanced liquid feed monthly in spring and summer. None in winter.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Causes oral irritation, drooling and vomiting if chewed.

problems.sign: Leaves stay whole with no splits
problems.cause: Not enough light, or plant is still juvenile
problems.fix: Move closer to a bright window. Splits develop with maturity.

problems.cause: Overwatering
problems.fix: Let the top layer dry fully before the next drink. Check that drainage is not blocked.

problems.cause: Dry air or underwatering
problems.fix: Water more consistently; group with other plants to raise local humidity.

species.note: Aerial roots are normal and healthy. Tuck them into the pot or leave them; do not cut them off.

species.light: Bright indirect. No direct sun.
species.water: Water when the top inch is dry. Dries faster than M. deliciosa because of thinner leaves.
species.soil: Airy mix with bark and perlite.
species.feeding: Balanced liquid feed monthly, spring through summer.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Oral irritation and vomiting if chewed.

problems.cause: Insufficient light
problems.fix: Move brighter. Leggy growth will not fill back in — prune and propagate instead.

problems.cause: Low humidity
problems.fix: Raise ambient humidity; avoid placing near heating vents.

species.note: Give it something to climb. Vining up a pole produces larger leaves with more holes than trailing down.

species.light: Adapts from low to bright indirect. Variegation fades in low light.
species.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out. Tolerates neglect far better than overwatering.
species.soil: Standard potting mix with added perlite.
species.feeding: Dilute balanced feed every 6-8 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Oral irritation, drooling, vomiting if chewed.

problems.cause: Too little light
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light. Prune back to a variegated node.

problems.cause: Root rot from overwatering
problems.fix: Unpot, cut away rotted roots, repot in fresh dry mix. Propagate healthy cuttings as insurance.

species.note: The most forgiving plant on this list. If you kill a pothos, the cause is almost always too much water, not too little.

species.light: Anything from low light to full sun. Grows fastest in bright indirect.
species.water: Let the soil dry completely, then water sparingly. Every 2-6 weeks depending on light and season.
species.soil: Cactus or succulent mix. Drainage is critical.
species.feeding: Succulent feed twice during the growing season at most.
species.toxic_note: Saponins. Causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea if eaten.

problems.cause: Overwatering — the most common way this plant dies
problems.fix: Stop watering. Remove affected leaves at the base. Repot into dry gritty mix.

problems.cause: Genuinely underwatered
problems.fix: Water thoroughly once; leaves plump up over several days.

species.note: In winter it may need water only once a month. When in doubt, wait another week.

species.light: Low to bright indirect. One of the few genuinely low-light-tolerant plants.
species.water: Every 2-4 weeks, only once the soil is dry throughout. Stores water in its rhizomes.
species.soil: Well-draining potting mix with perlite or a cactus blend.
species.feeding: Dilute feed twice a year. It barely needs it.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Oral irritation and vomiting if chewed.

problems.cause: Overwatering
problems.fix: Stop watering entirely until the soil is bone dry. Check rhizomes for soft spots.

problems.cause: Normal — it is a slow grower
problems.fix: Nothing. Brighter light speeds it up slightly.

species.note: The best plant for a dark office or a forgetful owner. Almost impossible to underwater.

species.light: Bright light, including some direct morning sun. Needs more light than most people give it.
species.water: When the top 2 inches are dry. Consistency matters more than volume — it hates swings.
species.soil: Well-draining potting mix.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Ficus sap irritates skin, mouth and gut. Causes vomiting and drooling if chewed.

problems.sign: Brown spots spreading from leaf edges
problems.cause: Usually overwatering or root rot
problems.fix: Check roots. Let it dry further between waterings.

problems.cause: Shock from being moved, a draft, or a temperature swing
problems.fix: Pick one bright spot and leave it there. It dislikes being relocated.

species.note: The hardest plant here. It wants one bright position, a consistent watering rhythm, and no drafts. Pick its spot carefully and then stop fussing.

species.light: Bright indirect. Variegated forms need more light than plain green.
species.water: When the top 2 inches dry out. Less in winter.
species.soil: Well-draining potting mix with perlite.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Milky latex sap. Irritates mouth and gut; causes vomiting if chewed.

problems.cause: Overwatering or a cold draft
problems.fix: Let the soil dry further; move away from drafty windows and doors.

problems.cause: Dust buildup blocks light
problems.fix: Wipe leaves with a damp cloth monthly. Makes a visible difference.

species.note: Far more forgiving than its cousin the fiddle leaf fig, and nearly as striking.

species.light: Low to bright indirect. Blooms more in brighter light; survives in dim corners.
species.water: Keep lightly moist. It wilts dramatically when thirsty and recovers within hours of watering.
species.soil: Standard potting mix that holds some moisture.
species.feeding: Dilute feed every 6-8 weeks in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Oral irritation, drooling, difficulty swallowing. Not a true lily and not kidney-toxic to cats, unlike Lilium.

problems.cause: Underwatered
problems.fix: Water thoroughly. It usually recovers completely within a few hours.

problems.cause: Tap water minerals, fluoride, or dry air
problems.fix: Try filtered or left-out water; raise humidity.

problems.cause: Too little light
problems.fix: Move to brighter indirect light.

species.note: Its wilting is a useful signal, not a crisis — this is the one plant that reliably tells you when it is thirsty.

species.light: Bright indirect. Rotate weekly or it leans hard toward the light.
species.water: When the top inch is dry. Leaves droop slightly when thirsty.
species.soil: Well-draining potting mix.
species.feeding: Dilute feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Phototropism — normal
problems.fix: Rotate a quarter turn weekly.

problems.cause: Too much direct sun
problems.fix: Move back from the glass into indirect light.

species.note: Produces pups at the base that can be separated and potted. One plant becomes many within a year.

species.light: Bright indirect to some direct sun. More light means tighter spacing and stronger colour.
species.water: Let the soil dry fully. Semi-succulent — it stores water in its leaves and tubers.
species.soil: Cactus or succulent mix.
species.feeding: Dilute succulent feed twice in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Too little light
problems.fix: Move brighter. Trim long bare sections and lay cuttings on soil to root.

problems.cause: Overwatering
problems.fix: Let it dry out completely; reduce frequency.

species.note: Hang it high. Vines reach several feet and the heart shape only reads properly when it trails.

species.light: Medium to bright indirect. Variegation needs light to hold.
species.water: When the top inch is dry.
species.soil: Well-draining potting mix with perlite.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Oral irritation and vomiting if chewed.

problems.cause: Not enough light
problems.fix: Move brighter; cut back to a well-variegated node.

problems.cause: Low light
problems.fix: Brighter position and pinch the tips to encourage branching.

species.note: Nearly as tough as pothos but with better colour. Pinch growing tips to keep it full rather than stringy.

species.light: Medium indirect. Direct sun bleaches the silver banding.
species.water: Keep evenly moist, never soggy, never bone dry. Use filtered or dechlorinated water.
species.humidity: 60%+. This is non-negotiable for good leaves.
species.soil: Moisture-retentive but airy mix with peat or coir and perlite.
species.feeding: Dilute feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs. One of the safest statement plants for pet homes.

problems.cause: Low humidity or hard tap water
problems.fix: Raise humidity above 60%; switch to filtered water.

problems.cause: Underwatered or too dry an atmosphere
problems.fix: Water and raise humidity together.

species.note: Demanding about humidity and water quality. Genuinely pet-safe, which is why people persist with it.

species.light: Medium indirect. Avoid direct sun.
species.water: Keep evenly moist. Filtered water preferred.
species.soil: Moisture-retentive airy mix.
species.feeding: Dilute feed every 4-6 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.sign: Leaves folded up and staying up
problems.cause: Normal at night; if constant, it is thirsty or the air is too dry
problems.fix: Check soil moisture and humidity.

problems.cause: Too much light
problems.fix: Move further from the window.

species.note: Leaves fold upward at night and open in the morning. The movement is normal and worth watching for.

species.light: Bright indirect. No direct sun.
species.water: Keep lightly moist in summer; reduce sharply in winter. Hates sitting wet.
species.soil: Airy, fast-draining mix with bark and perlite.
species.feeding: Dilute feed monthly in spring and summer only.
species.toxic_note: High insoluble calcium oxalate content. Significant oral irritation, drooling and swelling if chewed.

problems.sign: Dropping all its leaves in autumn
problems.cause: Often natural dormancy, not death
problems.fix: Reduce water, keep the corm warm and barely moist, wait for spring.

problems.cause: Spider mites — Alocasia are highly prone
problems.fix: Rinse leaves, treat with insecticidal soap weekly for three weeks, raise humidity.

species.note: Check the undersides of leaves weekly. Spider mites find this plant faster than any other on the list.

species.light: Low to medium indirect. Direct sun scorches the fronds.
species.water: Keep lightly moist. Water the soil, not the central rosette — water sitting in the crown rots it.
species.soil: Moisture-retentive, airy mix.
species.feeding: Dilute feed every 6-8 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Dry air
problems.fix: Raise humidity; move away from vents and radiators.

problems.sign: Rot at the centre of the rosette
problems.cause: Water poured into the crown
problems.fix: Always water the soil around the edge of the pot instead.

species.note: The easiest fern to keep alive indoors, and safe around pets. Never water into the middle.

species.light: Bright indirect. Tolerates medium light.
species.water: When the top inch dries. Sensitive to fluoride in tap water.
species.soil: Standard potting mix.
species.feeding: Dilute feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Not toxic to cats or dogs. Cats are often drawn to chewing it; this causes no poisoning, though large amounts may upset the stomach.

problems.cause: Fluoride or chlorine in tap water
problems.fix: Use filtered water or leave tap water out overnight.

problems.cause: Too little light, or pot too large
problems.fix: Brighter light; spider plants pup more readily when slightly root-bound.

species.note: Pet-safe and prolific. The plantlets root in water in about two weeks, which makes it the best plant to give away.

species.light: Bright light with some direct sun.
species.water: Soak thoroughly, then let the soil dry completely. Every 2-4 weeks.
species.soil: Cactus or succulent mix with grit.
species.feeding: Succulent feed once or twice in summer.
species.toxic_note: Saponins and anthraquinones in the leaf skin and latex. Causes vomiting, diarrhoea and lethargy if eaten by cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Too little light
problems.fix: Move to the brightest spot available.

problems.cause: Overwatering
problems.fix: Stop watering. Remove affected leaves. Repot in gritty dry mix if the base is soft.

species.note: Toxic to pets despite being a household remedy for humans. Worth stating plainly on the card.

species.light: Bright light with several hours of direct sun.
species.water: Let the soil dry fully between waterings. Every 2-3 weeks in summer, monthly or less in winter.
species.soil: Cactus or succulent mix.
species.feeding: Succulent feed twice in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Toxic to cats and dogs. Causes vomiting, incoordination and lethargy. The toxic principle is not fully identified.

problems.cause: Usually overwatering; sometimes a sudden move
problems.fix: Let it dry out thoroughly and reduce frequency.

problems.cause: Not enough light
problems.fix: Move to direct sun. Prune leggy growth; cuttings root easily.

species.note: Can live for decades and be pruned like a bonsai. Treat it as a sun plant, not a shelf plant.

species.light: Bright indirect with some direct sun. Light drives flowering.
species.water: Let the top half dry out. Semi-succulent leaves store water.
species.soil: Chunky, free-draining mix with bark and perlite.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Too little light, or the old flower spurs were cut off
problems.fix: More light. Never remove the short leafless spurs — flowers rebloom from them.

problems.cause: Underwatered or root-bound
problems.fix: Water thoroughly; check whether roots fill the pot.

species.note: Do not deadhead. Flowers return from the same woody spurs year after year, and cutting them off costs you next season's blooms.

species.light: Bright indirect. No direct sun.
species.water: Keep lightly moist; let the top inch dry between waterings.
species.soil: Very chunky orchid-style mix with bark — it is semi-epiphytic.
species.feeding: High-phosphorus feed diluted, every 6-8 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Oral irritation, drooling and swelling if chewed.

problems.cause: Normal ageing of the spathe, or too little light
problems.fix: Nothing if the bloom is old. Otherwise increase light.

problems.cause: Overwatering in too dense a substrate
problems.fix: Repot into a chunkier, barkier mix.

species.note: The red 'flower' is a modified leaf and lasts weeks. Plant it in bark, not dense soil — most Anthurium deaths are a potting mix problem.

species.light: Low to medium indirect. One of the best true low-light plants.
species.water: Keep lightly moist; let the top inch dry. Sensitive to both extremes.
species.soil: Standard potting mix with perlite.
species.feeding: Dilute feed every 8 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Dry air or fluoride in tap water
problems.fix: Raise humidity; use filtered water. Trim tips with scissors.

problems.cause: Spider mites, common in dry air
problems.fix: Rinse thoroughly, treat with insecticidal soap, raise humidity.

species.note: Pet-safe, genuinely tolerates low light, and stays a manageable size. The best palm for a dim room.

species.light: Medium to bright indirect.
species.water: Let the top half dry. Thick leaves store water — it behaves semi-succulent.
species.soil: Well-draining mix with perlite.
species.feeding: Dilute feed every 6-8 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Overwatering
problems.fix: Let it dry out further between waterings.

problems.cause: Too little light
problems.fix: Brighter indirect light; pinch tips to encourage bushiness.

species.note: Compact, pet-safe and very hard to kill. An excellent desk plant and a good first plant for a cat household.

species.light: Medium to bright indirect. Direct sun fades the striping.
species.water: Let the top half dry out.
species.soil: Well-draining mix with perlite.
species.feeding: Dilute feed every 6-8 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Thirsty, or overwatered — check the soil before acting
problems.fix: If dry, water. If wet, let it dry out fully.

problems.cause: Too much direct light
problems.fix: Move back from the window.

species.note: Leaf cuttings with a short stalk root readily in water. Pet-safe and compact.

species.light: Bright indirect. No soil, no pot.
species.water: Soak in room-temperature water for 20-30 minutes every 1-2 weeks, then shake out and dry upside down within 4 hours.
species.humidity: 50%+. Mist between soaks in dry homes.
species.soil: None. Mount on wood or display in a bowl with airflow.
species.feeding: Dilute bromeliad feed in the soak water once a month.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.sign: Rotting, falling apart at the base
problems.cause: Water trapped in the centre after soaking
problems.fix: Always dry upside down with good airflow. Never leave it sitting wet in a closed terrarium.

problems.cause: Not enough water
problems.fix: Soak more often; mist between soaks.

species.note: The drying step matters more than the watering step. Rot from trapped water kills more air plants than drought does.

species.light: Bright indirect. Needs more light than plain green pothos to hold its white variegation.
species.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out. Grows slower than golden pothos, so it drinks less.
species.soil: Standard potting mix with added perlite.
species.feeding: Dilute balanced feed every 6-8 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Oral irritation, drooling and vomiting if chewed.

problems.sign: New leaves coming in mostly green
problems.cause: Not enough light to support the white sections
problems.fix: Move brighter. Prune back to a well-marbled node.

problems.sign: Brown crisping on the white parts first
problems.cause: Sun scorch - white tissue burns before green does
problems.fix: Pull back from direct sun into bright indirect.

species.note: The white parts carry no chlorophyll, so this grows noticeably slower than golden pothos. That is normal, not a problem.

species.light: The brightest spot you have, including several hours of direct sun. It is a full-sun plant outdoors.
species.water: Water thoroughly when the top 2 inches dry. Large leaves move a lot of water in summer.
species.soil: Rich, well-draining potting mix.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly spring through summer. It is a heavy feeder for a houseplant.
species.toxic_note: Toxic to cats and dogs. The seeds and fruit are the worst part. Causes vomiting and drowsiness.

problems.cause: Completely normal - it is how the plant survives wind
problems.fix: Nothing. Splits are not damage and cannot be prevented.

problems.cause: Not enough light. This is the usual indoor failure.
problems.fix: Move to the brightest window in the house. It cannot thrive in medium light.

species.note: Indoor plants rarely flower - they typically need several years, a lot of direct sun, and to be root-bound. Treat it as a foliage plant.

species.light: Bright indirect. The white pinstripes fade without it.
species.water: When the top inch is dry.
species.soil: Airy mix with bark and perlite.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Oral irritation and vomiting if chewed.

problems.cause: Low light, or natural instability - Birkin is a mutation and can revert
problems.fix: Increase light. Cut the reverted stem back below the green growth.

problems.sign: A fully white leaf that then dies
problems.cause: No chlorophyll in that leaf, so it cannot sustain itself
problems.fix: Normal. Remove it once it yellows; the plant is fine.

species.note: Birkin is a mutation, so no two leaves stripe identically and occasional reversion is built in rather than something you did wrong.

species.light: Bright indirect, and plenty of it. Light drives the pink.
species.water: When the top inch is dry. Do not let it sit wet.
species.soil: Chunky aroid mix with bark, perlite and a little coir.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Insoluble calcium oxalates. Oral irritation, drooling and vomiting if chewed.

problems.cause: Too little light, or the plant is reverting
problems.fix: More bright indirect light. Prune back to a node showing variegation.

problems.sign: An entirely pink leaf that browns and dies
problems.cause: No chlorophyll, so the leaf cannot feed itself
problems.fix: Expected. Do not chase all-pink leaves - a half-and-half leaf is the healthy ideal.

species.note: Aim for roughly half pink per leaf. Fully pink leaves look spectacular in photos and then die, because they have no chlorophyll.

species.light: Medium indirect. Direct sun bleaches the pattern.
species.water: Keep evenly moist with filtered or dechlorinated water. Never soggy, never bone dry.
species.soil: Moisture-retentive but airy mix.
species.feeding: Dilute feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Dry air or minerals in tap water
problems.fix: Raise humidity above 60%. Switch to filtered or distilled water.

problems.cause: Thirsty, or the air is too dry
problems.fix: Water and raise humidity together - usually both are involved.

species.note: The undersides are deep purple and the leaves lift at night, so it is worth a spot where you see it from more than one angle.

species.light: Bright indirect. No direct sun on the leaves.
species.water: Lightly moist in summer, much drier in winter. Hates sitting wet.
species.soil: Very airy, fast-draining mix with bark and perlite.
species.feeding: Dilute feed monthly in spring and summer only.
species.toxic_note: High insoluble calcium oxalate content. Significant oral irritation, drooling and swelling if chewed.

problems.cause: Spider mites, which target Alocasia relentlessly
problems.fix: Rinse both leaf surfaces, treat with insecticidal soap weekly for three weeks, raise humidity.

problems.cause: Usually dormancy, not death
problems.fix: Cut water right back, keep the corm warm and barely damp, wait for spring.

species.note: The striped stems are the point - give it room so they are visible rather than crowded against other plants.

species.light: Bright indirect. No direct sun.
species.water: Keep consistently moist. This is one of the few houseplants that genuinely dislikes drying out.
species.humidity: 60%+. The single biggest factor in whether it thrives.
species.soil: Moisture-retentive peat or coir based mix.
species.feeding: Dilute feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.sign: Dropping leaflets all over the floor
problems.cause: Air too dry, or it dried out once too often
problems.fix: Raise humidity, water more consistently, move away from heating vents.

problems.cause: Too much direct light
problems.fix: Move to bright indirect or filtered light.

species.note: Pet-safe and genuinely lush, but it wants humidity more than any other plant here. A bathroom with a window is close to ideal.

species.light: Medium indirect. Direct sun kills it quickly.
species.water: Never let it dry out, not even once. Keep the soil evenly damp at all times.
species.soil: Moisture-retentive, airy mix.
species.feeding: Very dilute feed every 6-8 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: It dried out, or the air is too dry
problems.fix: Cut the dead fronds right back to soil level, water, raise humidity. It regrows from the base.

problems.cause: Often dormant rather than gone
problems.fix: Trim everything to the soil, keep it damp and warm, and give it a month before giving up.

species.note: The least forgiving plant in the shop. One missed watering can take out every frond, though it usually regrows from the base if you cut back and keep it damp.

species.light: As much direct sun as you can give it. At least 6 hours.
species.water: Soak thoroughly, then let the soil dry out completely. Water the soil, not the rosette.
species.soil: Gritty cactus or succulent mix. Drainage is everything.
species.feeding: Dilute succulent feed twice in summer at most.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.sign: Stretching tall with gaps between leaves
problems.cause: Not enough light - the most common indoor problem
problems.fix: Move to the sunniest spot. Behead the stretched rosette and re-root the top.

problems.cause: Overwatering, or water sitting in the rosette
problems.fix: Stop watering until bone dry. Always water the soil, never the centre.

species.note: Pet-safe and nearly indestructible given enough sun. The powdery coating on the leaves is a natural sunscreen, so handle by the pot rather than the leaves.

species.light: Bright indirect to a little direct sun. More tolerant of lower light than most succulents.
species.water: Let the soil dry completely, then water sparingly. Every 2-3 weeks in summer, monthly in winter.
species.soil: Gritty cactus or succulent mix.
species.feeding: Dilute succulent feed once or twice in summer.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Overwatering
problems.fix: Stop watering. Remove mushy leaves. Repot into dry gritty mix if the base is soft.

problems.sign: Red or purple tinge to the leaves
problems.cause: Sun stress - usually harmless
problems.fix: Nothing needed unless leaves are also scorching, in which case reduce direct sun.

species.note: One of the best desk plants there is: pet-safe, happy in a small pot, tolerant of less light than most succulents, and nearly impossible to underwater.

species.light: Bright indirect with some direct sun.
species.water: Let the soil dry out almost completely. The thick leaves store water.
species.soil: Chunky, free-draining mix with bark and perlite.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: A single-leaf cutting sold without a node cannot produce a vine
problems.fix: Nothing will fix it. It can live for years as a leaf but will never become a plant.

problems.cause: Underwatered or root-bound
problems.fix: Water thoroughly and check whether roots fill the pot.

species.note: The single heart-shaped leaf sold as a gift is usually just a leaf with no growth node, so it will stay one leaf forever. Buy one with a vine attached if you want an actual plant.

species.light: Medium to bright indirect. Tolerates lower light with slower growth.
species.water: When the top inch is dry.
species.soil: Standard potting mix with perlite.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Among the more severe. High calcium oxalate content causes intense oral pain, drooling and swelling that can affect swallowing. Keep well away from pets and small children.

problems.sign: Bare leggy stem with leaves only at the top
problems.cause: Normal with age, accelerated by low light
problems.fix: Cut the cane back hard. It resprouts from the stump, and the cut top roots in water.

problems.cause: Overwatering or natural leaf drop
problems.fix: Let the soil dry further between waterings.

species.note: This is the one on the list worth being genuinely careful with. The sap causes painful mouth swelling, which is where the old name dumb cane comes from. Wash your hands after pruning.

species.light: Bright light with some direct sun. Colour is entirely light-dependent.
species.water: Keep lightly moist. Let the top inch dry, no more.
species.soil: Well-draining potting mix.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: The milky sap irritates skin, mouth and gut. Causes vomiting and drooling if chewed.

problems.sign: Dropping all its leaves after you bring it home
problems.cause: Shock from the change in light and humidity
problems.fix: Pick a bright spot and leave it alone. New growth usually follows within a few weeks.

problems.sign: New leaves coming in plain green
problems.cause: Not enough light
problems.fix: Move brighter. The reds and yellows only develop with strong light.

species.note: Expect it to drop leaves when you first bring it home. That is shock, not death, and it recovers if you stop moving it around.

species.light: Medium to bright indirect. Tolerates lower light with slower growth.
species.water: Let the top half of the pot dry out. Sensitive to fluoride in tap water.
species.soil: Well-draining potting mix.
species.feeding: Dilute feed every 8 weeks in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Saponins. Causes vomiting, drooling and loss of appetite. Cats may also show dilated pupils.

problems.sign: Brown tips on otherwise healthy leaves
problems.cause: Fluoride and salts in tap water
problems.fix: Use filtered or distilled water. Trim tips at an angle with scissors.

problems.cause: Normal ageing at the base of the cane
problems.fix: Nothing. Remove them once fully yellow.

species.note: Very tolerant of neglect but genuinely fussy about tap water. If the tips keep browning despite good watering, the water is the cause.

species.light: Bright indirect, with a little direct morning sun tolerated.
species.water: Keep lightly moist in summer, drier in winter. Sensitive to fluoride.
species.soil: Well-draining potting mix with perlite.
species.feeding: Balanced feed monthly in spring and summer.
species.toxic_note: Not known to be toxic to cats or dogs.

problems.cause: Dry air, or fluoride and salts in tap water
problems.fix: Raise humidity and switch to filtered water.

problems.cause: Spider mites, which love dry indoor air
problems.fix: Rinse thoroughly, treat with insecticidal soap, raise humidity.

species.note: One of the largest genuinely pet-safe plants you can keep indoors, which is why it turns up in so many homes with cats.

species.light: Bright light including a few hours of direct sun.
species.water: Let the soil dry completely, then water sparingly. More die from overwatering than anything else.
species.soil: Gritty cactus or succulent mix in a shallow pot.
species.feeding: Dilute succulent feed twice in the growing season.
species.toxic_note: Toxic to cats and dogs. Causes vomiting, drooling and skin irritation on contact.

problems.cause: Underwatered, or roots have died from earlier overwatering
problems.fix: Water thoroughly once. If there is no improvement in a week, check the roots.

problems.cause: Overwatering
problems.fix: Stop watering. Cut healthy strands and lay them on dry soil to re-root.

species.note: The roots are shallow, so a deep pot holds wet soil under them and rots the plant. Use a shallow pot and water less than feels right.
